questions.q: Show me your GitHub repositories.
questions.followup: Why did you build this one, and what would you do differently today?
questions.answer: Open 2-3 pinned repos you can explain well, each with a clear README (what it does, how to run it, a screenshot). For each one say the problem, your design choices, the tech stack and what you would change now (for example add tests, CI, better error handling or evals). Interviewers look for real commits over time, clean structure and honest reflection.

questions.q: Show me websites you have created.
questions.followup: Why did you choose that tech stack and hosting?
questions.answer: Show a live site, then explain the stack and why: for example a static site on GitHub Pages or Cloudflare for speed, low cost and simple deploys, or Next.js on Vercel when you need server code. Mention the domain, HTTPS, analytics, how you deploy (push to main runs tests then deploys) and what you would improve (accessibility, performance, SEO).

questions.q: Show me the tools you use.
questions.followup: Why these tools over the alternatives?
questions.answer: Group them: AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), coding (VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot), automation (n8n, Zapier), data and notes (Notion, NotebookLM), and cloud. For each say what job it does and why you picked it over alternatives: quality for your tasks, price, integrations, privacy and team standard. Show that you review tools from time to time instead of following hype.

questions.q: Show me the AI skills and extensions you have installed.
questions.followup: Why did you need each one, and how did it change the way you work?
questions.answer: Show your setup, for example IDE AI extensions, MCP servers (GitHub, browser, database), custom instructions or skills, and browser extensions. For each, explain the gap it filled (repeated manual steps, missing context, slow research) and the measurable change: faster reviews, fewer context switches, automated testing. Mention that you check permissions and data access before installing.

questions.q: Show me something you automated.
questions.followup: Why was it worth automating, and how much time or effort does it save?
questions.answer: Use a short story: the manual task (who did it, how often, how long), the automation (tools such as Python, n8n, Power Automate, Ansible or GitHub Actions), and the result in numbers, for example "4 hours a week saved, errors dropped to zero". Explain why it was worth it: frequent, rule-based, error-prone work. Mention monitoring and a human check where mistakes are costly.

questions.q: Show me a chatbot you built.
questions.followup: Why did you design it that way, and how do you handle wrong answers?
questions.answer: Describe the use case, the model, the knowledge source (RAG over documents), the interface and the guardrails. Explain design choices: RAG to ground answers, a system prompt that limits scope, citations, and refusing when unsure. For wrong answers: evals before release, user feedback buttons, logging and tracing, a fallback to a human, and regular prompt or data updates.

questions.q: Tell me about a project you are proud of.
questions.followup: Why are you proud of it, and what was the hardest part?
questions.answer: Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Pick a project with real impact and your clear role. Name the hardest part (a technical blocker, unclear requirements, a tight deadline) and exactly how you solved it. End with the result in numbers and what you learned.

questions.q: Have you been part of creating an AI strategy?
questions.followup: Why did the organization need it, and how was success measured?
questions.answer: Explain the why (stay competitive, cut costs, use data better, manage risk), then the parts: business goals, high-value use cases ranked by value and feasibility, data readiness, build vs buy, governance and responsible AI, skills and training, and a roadmap with quick wins. Success measures: adoption, time or cost saved, revenue impact, quality and risk metrics. If you have not done it, describe how you would.

questions.q: Have you been a project manager on an AI project?
questions.followup: Why did the project succeed or struggle, and what did you learn?
questions.answer: Describe scope, team, timeline and your role. AI projects succeed with a clear business metric, good data early, a small pilot, evals and stakeholder buy-in. They struggle with poor data, unclear success criteria, scope creep and no plan for production. Share one concrete lesson, such as building the eval set before the model.

questions.q: Can you recall some recent AI news you read or explored?
questions.followup: Why does it matter, and how could it affect our business?
questions.answer: Pick one recent, specific item (a model release, a regulation such as the EU AI Act, a chip or a funding deal) and summarize it in two sentences. Then connect it to the business: cost, new capability, risk or competition, and suggest one action, such as running a pilot or reviewing compliance.

questions.q: Is there a feature, product, tool or invention you really admire?
questions.followup: Why that one over the others, and how would you improve it?
questions.answer: Choose something specific and explain the problem it solves and why it is better than alternatives (simplicity, design, impact). Then suggest a realistic improvement. This shows product thinking: users, trade-offs and iteration.

questions.q: How do you use AI in your day-to-day work?
questions.followup: Why do you trust its output, and how do you check it?
questions.answer: Give concrete examples: drafting and editing, coding and code review, research and summarizing, data analysis, meeting notes and automation. You trust but verify: check facts against sources, run and test code, ask for citations, compare two models for important work, and never paste confidential data into tools that are not approved.

questions.q: What is the difference between a graph database and a vector database?
questions.followup: Why would you use both together in one AI system, for example in GraphRAG?
questions.answer: A graph database (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) stores entities as nodes and relationships as edges; it answers questions about connections ("who reports to whom", multi-hop paths) with exact queries. A vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector, FAISS) stores embeddings and finds items by meaning (similarity search). Together, as in GraphRAG: vectors find relevant passages, and the graph adds linked facts and relationships, improving answers that need several connected facts.

questions.q: Have you used Hugging Face, and how?
questions.followup: Why did you choose those models, datasets or Spaces, and how did you evaluate them?
questions.answer: Describe real use: downloading open models with Transformers, using datasets, building demos in Spaces, fine-tuning with PEFT/LoRA, or calling Inference Endpoints. Explain choices: model size vs hardware, license, benchmark and leaderboard results, downloads and community activity, and then your own evals on your data comparing quality, speed and cost.

questions.q: What is LangChain, and how do LangGraph and LangSmith fit with it?
questions.followup: When would you skip LangChain and call the model API directly, and why?
questions.answer: LangChain is an open-source framework with building blocks for LLM apps: model wrappers, prompts, tools, retrievers and many integrations. LangGraph builds stateful agent workflows as graphs with loops, memory, checkpoints and human-in-the-loop. LangSmith traces, evaluates and monitors LLM apps (even ones not built with LangChain). Skip LangChain for simple apps: a direct API call with the official SDK is easier to read, debug and keep up to date.

questions.q: Name the main parts of the Hugging Face ecosystem and what each is for.
questions.followup: How would you take an open model from the Hub to a production API?
questions.answer: Hub: hosts models, datasets and Spaces. Spaces: demo apps (Gradio, Streamlit). Transformers: library to load and run pretrained models. Datasets: load and share data. PEFT: LoRA and other efficient fine-tuning. TGI (Text Generation Inference): production serving. smolagents: small code-writing agents. To production: pick and evaluate the model, quantize if needed, serve it with TGI or vLLM in a container on GPUs (or Inference Endpoints), put an API gateway in front, and add monitoring, autoscaling and rate limits.

questions.q: What is Liquid AI, and how are its Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) different from Transformer LLMs?
questions.followup: When would you pick a small on-device model like LFM2 over a large cloud model such as GPT or Claude?
questions.answer: Liquid AI is a Boston-based MIT spin-off (Ramin Hasani, Mathias Lechner, Alexander Amini, Daniela Rus). Its Liquid Foundation Models are not plain Transformers: they come from liquid neural network research and use efficient designs (for example LFM2 mixes short convolutions with a few attention layers), giving low memory use and fast speed on phones, laptops and edge devices as well as in the cloud. Pick a small on-device model for privacy, offline use, low latency and low cost on simple, high-volume tasks; pick a large cloud model for hard reasoning and broad knowledge.

questions.q: What are the weights of an LLM, and how are they created and used?
questions.followup: What changes in the weights when you fine-tune with LoRA, and why do companies treat weights as their most valuable asset?
questions.answer: Weights are the billions of numbers (parameters, together with biases) a model learns in training; "70B" means about 70 billion of them. They sit in matrices: token embeddings, attention (Q, K, V, O), feed-forward layers and the output head. Training starts them random, then backpropagation and an optimizer such as Adam adjust them to reduce next-token prediction error over trillions of tokens. At inference the weights are frozen and only read. Knowledge is spread across them, not stored as text. LoRA freezes the original weights and trains small low-rank matrices added to some layers, so it needs little memory and the adapter is tiny. Weights are valuable because they hold the result of very expensive training (data, compute, know-how); the code is small, so whoever has the weights has the model, which is why some companies keep them closed and others release them as open weights.

questions.q: Compare open-weight LLMs (for example Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Gemma, GLM) with closed models used only through an API (for example GPT, Claude, Gemini). What are the pros and cons of each?
questions.followup: For a bank chatbot that handles customer data, which would you choose and why? What would change for a small startup prototype?
questions.answer: Open-weight: you download and run the model yourself. Pros: data stays on your servers (privacy, compliance, data residency), full control of versions (no surprise changes or retirement), fine-tuning, offline or edge use, no per-token fee and no vendor lock-in. Cons: you pay for GPUs and engineering (serving, scaling, security, updates), the best open models are often a step behind the top closed ones on the hardest tasks, and licenses vary (Apache 2.0 and MIT are permissive; some add limits). Closed API models: pros are top quality, no infrastructure, fast start, built-in tools (search, vision, voice) and the vendor's safety and uptime; cons are per-token cost that grows with volume, data leaves your network, rate limits, the vendor can change or retire models, and lock-in. Open-weight is not the same as open source: training data and code are often private. For a bank: self-host an open model (or use a closed model through a private cloud deal with no data retention) because of privacy and regulation, and run evals to check quality. For a startup prototype: start with a closed API for speed and quality, then move high-volume or sensitive tasks to an open model when cost or privacy matters. Many teams mix both and route each task to the cheapest model that passes their evals.

questions.q: What kinds of decision models do you know, and when would you use each?
questions.followup: How would you explain a model's decision to a regulator or an affected customer?
questions.answer: Rules and decision tables (DMN) for clear, auditable business logic; decision trees for simple, explainable predictions; ensembles (random forests, gradient boosting) for accurate predictions on tabular data; expected utility and influence diagrams for choices under uncertainty; MDPs and reinforcement learning for decisions over many steps; multi-criteria methods (weighted scoring, AHP) for trade-offs. To explain to a regulator or customer: use interpretable models or explanation tools (SHAP, reason codes), give the main factors in plain language, document data and testing, and offer a human review and appeal.

questions.q: How do you turn a model's prediction into a business decision, for example choosing the threshold for a fraud or loan model?
questions.followup: When should a human review the decision, and how would you check it for bias?
questions.answer: A model outputs a probability; the decision is the threshold. Choose it from the cost of each error (a missed fraud vs a false alarm), using the confusion matrix, precision/recall and expected cost, often with bands: auto-approve, auto-decline and a middle band for human review. Humans should review uncertain, high-impact or unusual cases. Check bias by comparing error rates and approval rates across groups, and monitor after launch.

questions.q: What is FLOPS?
questions.followup: Why can peak FLOPS be misleading when choosing a GPU for LLM inference?
questions.answer: FLOPS = floating-point operations per second, a measure of compute speed (TFLOPS = trillions, PFLOPS = quadrillions). Peak FLOPS is a best case at one precision (often FP8 or FP4, sometimes with sparsity). LLM token generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, not compute, so a GPU with more memory bandwidth and capacity can be faster for inference even with lower peak FLOPS.

questions.q: What chunking strategies or approaches do you know for RAG?
questions.followup: Why would you choose one chunking strategy over another, and how do chunk size and overlap affect retrieval quality and cost?
questions.answer: Fixed-size chunks (by tokens), recursive splitting (paragraphs, then sentences), sentence- or document-structure-based (headings, sections, tables), semantic chunking (split where meaning changes), overlap between chunks, and parent-child (search small chunks, return the larger parent). Small chunks give precise matches but lose context; large chunks keep context but add noise and cost more tokens. Overlap keeps ideas from being cut but adds storage. Choose by document type and test with retrieval evals (recall@k).

questions.q: What are the different types of RAG architectures and strategies?
questions.followup: Why would you pick a particular RAG architecture for a use case, and how would you evaluate whether it works?
questions.answer: Naive RAG (embed, retrieve top-k, generate); advanced RAG with query rewriting and re-ranking; hybrid search (keyword BM25 plus vectors); GraphRAG (knowledge graph for connected facts); agentic RAG (an agent decides what and when to search, possibly in several steps); multimodal RAG (images, tables, audio). Pick by need: simple FAQ → naive or hybrid; many linked entities → GraphRAG; complex multi-step questions → agentic. Evaluate retrieval (recall, precision) and answers (faithfulness, relevance) on a test set, plus latency and cost.

questions.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol) and how does it work?
questions.followup: Why use MCP instead of building a custom integration for every tool, and what security risks does it bring?
questions.answer: MCP is an open standard (from Anthropic) for connecting AI apps to tools and data. The host is the AI app; it runs one client per server connection; servers expose tools (actions), resources (data) and prompts (templates). Benefit: build an integration once and use it in any MCP-compatible app instead of custom code for each. Risks: prompt injection through tool results, over-broad permissions, untrusted servers and data leaks, so use least privilege, trusted servers, user approval for actions and logging.

questions.q: What is an AI agent, and which agent patterns do you know?
questions.followup: Why and when would you choose a simple fixed workflow over a fully autonomous agent?
questions.answer: An agent is an LLM that decides its own next steps and tool calls in a loop toward a goal. Patterns: ReAct (think, act, observe), prompt chaining, routing, orchestrator-workers (a lead model splits and delegates), evaluator-optimizer (one critiques, another improves), and multi-agent handoffs. Use a simple fixed workflow when the steps are known: it is cheaper, faster, more predictable and easier to test. Use an autonomous agent only when the path cannot be known in advance and the value is worth the extra risk.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an LLM application (evals)?
questions.followup: Why can't you rely on public benchmarks alone, and how do you make sure an LLM-as-a-judge is trustworthy?
questions.answer: Build an eval set from real tasks with expected results; score with code checks (exact match, JSON valid, tests pass), rubrics, LLM-as-a-judge and human review; track quality, latency and cost; run evals on every prompt or model change; and monitor production with tracing and user feedback. Public benchmarks don't match your tasks and can be contaminated. Make a judge trustworthy by testing it against human labels, using clear rubrics, and checking for bias (position, length, self-preference).

questions.q: Which benchmarks do you know for LLMs and for AI hardware, and what does each one measure?
questions.followup: Why can benchmark results be misleading (contamination, saturation, different setups), and how would you benchmark for your own use case?
questions.answer: LLMs: MMLU/MMLU-Pro (knowledge), GPQA (expert science), HumanEval and SWE-bench (coding), GSM8K and AIME (math), MMMU (multimodal), LMArena (human preference). Hardware: MLPerf Training and Inference (speed across systems). Results mislead through contamination (test data in training), saturation (top models all near 100%), and different settings (prompts, precision, batch size). For your use case, build your own eval set and measure quality, latency, throughput and cost on your hardware.

questions.q: What is "Tron", and how does it relate to Project Maven, Google, and the Maven Smart System?
questions.followup: Why did Google walk away from Project Maven, and what does that tell you about ethics and employee pressure when AI is used for defense?
questions.answer: Project Maven is the Pentagon's AI program (started 2017) for analysing drone and surveillance video. Google ran an early pilot, supplying TensorFlow tools, but dropped the contract in 2018 after thousands of employees protested and some resigned, and it published AI principles. Palantir then took over the work; "Tron" was Palantir's internal codename for it. Maven grew into the Maven Smart System used for targeting and intelligence. Lesson: employee values and public pressure can change company decisions, and defense AI needs clear ethics, oversight and human control.

questions.q: Name a research paper that had a high impact on AI or generative AI, and explain what it contributed.
questions.followup: Why was that paper a turning point, and how does its idea show up in the AI tools you use today?
questions.answer: Example: "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., Google, 2017) introduced the Transformer, using self-attention instead of recurrence, so training became parallel and models could scale. It is the base of GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama. Other good picks: AlexNet (2012, deep learning on GPUs), BERT (2018), GPT-3 (2020, few-shot learning), scaling laws (2020), InstructGPT/RLHF (2022), and diffusion models (2020).

questions.q: What is the single guardrail rule that could eliminate the chance of AI eliminating humans?
questions.followup: How about the guardrail "protect humans at any cost": if all AI vendors agreed on it and applied it, would it be enough to completely eliminate the chance of AI eliminating humans?
questions.answer: There is no single rule that fully removes the risk; a commonly suggested core rule is "AI must never act to harm humans or remove human control over AI" (keep humans in control, with the ability to stop it). "Protect humans at any cost" is not enough: it is vague (which humans, what counts as harm), "at any cost" can justify extreme actions such as restricting freedom "for our safety", rules can be misread or gamed, not every actor (including criminals or rival states) would apply it, and no one can yet prove that a model will reliably follow a rule. Real safety needs layers: alignment research, testing, monitoring, limits on autonomy, regulation and international agreements.

questions.q: Talk about the EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machine: what it does, who makes it, and why it matters for AI chips.
questions.followup: Why does a single supplier (ASML) for these machines matter for the AI hardware supply chain and for export controls?
questions.answer: EUV lithography machines print the tiniest chip patterns using 13.5 nm extreme ultraviolet light, made by firing lasers at tin droplets, focused with ultra-precise mirrors in a vacuum. Only ASML (Netherlands) makes them; each costs well over $150 million (high-NA versions even more). They are needed for the most advanced chips (about 7 nm and below), such as NVIDIA GPUs made by TSMC. A single supplier is a supply-chain choke point, and export controls on EUV machines are used to limit which countries can make leading-edge AI chips.

questions.q: What is the difference between Git and a GitHub repository?
questions.followup: Why would a team use GitHub (or GitLab) on top of Git, and how do pull requests and CI/CD fit in?
questions.answer: Git is a version control tool that runs on your computer: it tracks changes, branches and history. GitHub is a hosting service for Git repositories in the cloud, adding collaboration: pull requests, code review, issues, Actions (CI/CD), permissions and backups. Teams use GitHub or GitLab to share code and review changes: a developer pushes a branch, opens a pull request, CI runs tests automatically, reviewers approve, and merging can trigger deployment.

questions.q: In a few simple steps, explain how to convert a website (web app) into a mobile app.
questions.followup: Why would you choose a PWA, a wrapper like Capacitor, or a full rewrite in React Native or Flutter, and what changes for app store review and device features?
questions.answer: 1) Make the site responsive and mobile-friendly. 2) Quick option: turn it into a PWA (manifest plus service worker) so it can be installed and work offline. 3) For app stores: wrap it with Capacitor (or Cordova) to make iOS and Android apps and add native plugins (camera, push notifications). 4) For best performance and native feel: rebuild in React Native or Flutter. 5) Test on real devices, then publish to the App Store and Google Play. PWA is cheapest but limited on iOS and not in stores by default; wrappers are fast but app review may reject apps that are "just a website"; rewrites cost most but give full device access.

questions.q: What is Ansible, and what is an Ansible playbook? Describe a playbook you have written or would write.
questions.followup: Does it work across remote servers, and how does it connect to them and run tasks on many hosts at once?
questions.answer: Ansible (Red Hat) is an open-source automation tool for configuring servers, deploying apps and managing infrastructure. A playbook is a YAML file listing plays: which hosts, and which tasks (modules such as apt, copy, service) to run, written to be idempotent (safe to run again). Example: install nginx, copy the config, start the service on all web servers. Yes, it works across remote servers: it is agentless, connects over SSH (WinRM for Windows) using an inventory of hosts, and runs tasks on many hosts in parallel (controlled by forks).

questions.followup: Why would you choose that tool over the alternatives, and where would you add AI or a human check to the workflow?

questions.q: Define these 126 AI and tech terms, grouped by area.
questions.followup: Why does it matter to explain technical terms simply to non-technical stakeholders, and which of these do you use most in your work?
terms: Computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images or making decisions.
A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.
Machine learning with neural networks of many layers, which learn features directly from raw data.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
The field of AI focused on understanding and generating human language.
Hypothetical AI that matches or exceeds humans across most cognitive tasks.
A model of connected layers of artificial neurons; each connection has a weight that is adjusted during training.
The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the error by passing gradients backward through the network.
An optimization method that updates weights step by step in the direction that reduces the loss.
A formula that measures how wrong the model's predictions are; training tries to minimize it.
How big each weight update is during training; too high is unstable, too low is slow.
One full pass of the training data through the model.
The number of training examples processed together before one weight update.
When a model memorizes training data and performs poorly on new data.
Techniques (such as weight decay or dropout) that reduce overfitting by limiting model complexity.
Randomly switching off some neurons during training so the network does not rely on any single one.
A non-linear function (ReLU, GELU, sigmoid) applied to a neuron's output so networks can learn complex patterns.
A network using convolution filters to detect local patterns; the classic architecture for images.
A network that processes sequences step by step, carrying a hidden state from one step to the next.
A type of RNN with gates that help it remember information over long sequences.
The architecture behind modern LLMs; it uses self-attention to relate all tokens in a sequence in parallel.
A mechanism that lets each token weigh how relevant every other token is when building its representation.
An architecture with many expert sub-networks where a router activates only a few per token.
Two networks trained against each other: a generator creates fakes and a discriminator tries to spot them.
A generative model that encodes data into a probabilistic latent space and decodes samples from it.
A generative model that learns to turn random noise into data by reversing a gradual noising process.
A very large transformer model trained on huge text collections to understand and generate language.
A compact language model (usually a few billion parameters or fewer) that is cheaper and can run on devices.
A model that understands images together with text, for example answering questions about a picture.
A model that works with more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio and video.
A large model pretrained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks.
The basic unit of text a model reads and writes, often a word or part of a word.
The component that splits text into tokens and maps them to IDs (for example with byte pair encoding).
A dense vector of numbers representing the meaning of a token, sentence or item; similar meanings have nearby vectors.
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering input plus output.
A large, structured collection of texts used to train or study language models (corpora is the plural).
About meaning rather than exact wording; semantic search, for example, finds text with the same meaning even when the words differ.
A hierarchical classification scheme that organizes concepts into categories and sub-categories.
A formal model of concepts in a domain and the relationships between them, richer than a taxonomy.
The first, large-scale training stage where a model learns general knowledge, e.g. predicting the next token.
Further training of a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset.
Fine-tuning on instruction-response examples so a model follows user requests.
A fine-tuning method that freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices added to it.
Fine-tuning methods (like LoRA) that train only a small fraction of the parameters.
Training a smaller "student" model to imitate a larger "teacher" model's outputs.
Storing weights and activations with fewer bits (for example 8 or 4) to save memory and speed up inference.
Removing weights or neurons that contribute little, to make a model smaller and faster.
Artificially generated data (often by AI) used for training or testing.
Aligning a model using a reward model trained on human preference rankings, then optimizing the model with RL.
An alignment method that learns directly from preference pairs, without a separate reward model or RL loop.
A model that scores outputs according to learned human preferences; used in RLHF.
A design where humans review, correct or approve AI outputs or actions at key steps.
Making AI systems behave according to human intentions and values: helpful, honest and harmless.
Designing instructions and examples to get better, more reliable outputs from a model.
Asking a model to do a task without giving any examples.
Including a few worked examples in the prompt to show the model the task.
Having a model reason step by step before giving its final answer.
A sampling setting: higher values make outputs more random and creative, lower values more focused.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches p.
When a model produces confident output that is false or not supported by its sources.
Retrieving relevant documents and adding them to the prompt so the model answers from them.
A database optimized for storing embeddings and finding the most similar ones quickly.
Splitting documents into smaller pieces for embedding and retrieval in RAG.
Search by meaning (using embeddings) rather than by exact keywords.
Combining keyword search (like BM25) with semantic vector search for better retrieval.
A second step that re-scores retrieved results with a stronger model to put the best ones first.
A network of entities (nodes) and their relationships (edges).
RAG that uses a knowledge graph of entities and relationships to retrieve connected information.
An LLM-driven system that decides its own steps and uses tools in a loop to reach a goal.
A model outputting a structured request to run an external function or API, whose result is fed back.
An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data through servers that expose tools, resources and prompts.
An open protocol that lets AI agents communicate and collaborate with other agents.
Curating everything that goes into a model's context at each step: instructions, tools, data and history.
The software around a model that turns it into a working agent: it runs the loop, provides tools, manages context and memory, and enforces permissions (for example Claude Code or Codex CLI).
Designing the agent loop itself: how the model plans, acts, checks the result and decides to continue or stop, including retries, feedback and stopping conditions.
Designing systems where many AI agents work together, each with a role, handing tasks to one another and coordinating to reach a shared goal.
Checks and filters around a model that block unsafe, off-topic or malformed inputs and outputs.
An attack where malicious instructions hidden in input or retrieved content try to hijack the model.
A prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules.
A repeatable test that measures how well an AI system performs on a task.
A standard public test used to compare models or hardware (e.g. MMLU, SWE-bench, MLPerf).
Using an LLM to grade other models' outputs against a rubric or by comparing pairs.
How "surprised" a language model is by text; lower means it predicts the text better.
Using a trained model to make predictions or generate output.
The time from sending a request to getting the response (or the first token).
How much work a system completes per unit of time, such as tokens or requests per second.
Stored attention keys and values of previous tokens, so they are not recomputed at each generation step.
A processor with thousands of parallel cores; the main hardware for training and running AI models.
Google's custom chip designed for machine learning.
A chip in phones and PCs designed to run AI models efficiently on the device.
NVIDIA's platform and programming model for running general-purpose computation on its GPUs.
A unit in NVIDIA GPUs specialized for fast matrix multiply-accumulate, the core math of deep learning.
Stacked memory placed next to the GPU chip that provides very high memory bandwidth.
NVIDIA's high-speed interconnect for direct GPU-to-GPU communication.
Floating-point operations per second: a measure of computing speed (lowercase "FLOPs" often means a count of operations).
Training or inference that uses 16-bit number formats for speed while keeping key values in 32-bit.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: the world's largest contract chip manufacturer, which makes most leading AI chips, including NVIDIA GPUs.
Dutch company that builds the photolithography machines used to manufacture chips; the only supplier of EUV machines needed for the most advanced chips.
A model whose trained weights are published so anyone can download and run it.

An open-source license that lets you use, change and sell the code, even in closed-source products, as long as you keep the copyright and license notices. Apache 2.0 also grants contributors' patent rights; MIT is shorter and has no explicit patent grant.

An open-source license that lets you use and change the code, but if you distribute software built on it you must release the combined work under the same license, with source code. AGPL also applies when the software is offered as a network service (e.g. SaaS).
A pricing model where the basic product is free and users pay for premium features, higher limits or business plans (for example ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini free tiers).
A defined way for software to request services from other software, such as calling an LLM over the web.
A set of libraries and tools that make it easier to build on a platform or API.
A text-based interface where you type commands in a terminal (for example Claude Code or git).
A free, open-source operating system family; it runs most servers, cloud machines and AI training clusters.
A Windows feature that runs a real Linux environment inside Windows, popular for AI and developer tools.
A compatibility layer that lets Windows programs run on Linux and macOS without a Windows license (the name stands for "Wine Is Not an Emulator").
The package manager for Node.js (JavaScript): installs and manages libraries and runs project scripts.
The package installer for Python: installs libraries from PyPI, e.g. pip install torch.
A command-line tool for sending HTTP requests and transferring data, often used to test APIs.
The programming language of the web: runs in every browser and, with Node.js, on servers.
A dynamic, readable programming language, best known for the Ruby on Rails web framework.
A high-performance programming language for scientific and numerical computing, with Python-like syntax and near-C speed.
A high-level Python web framework for building web apps quickly, with a database ORM, admin panel and security features built in.
A lightweight text format for structured data using key-value pairs and lists; the standard format for APIs and LLM structured outputs.
A human-friendly data format that uses indentation instead of brackets; common for configuration files such as CI pipelines and Kubernetes.
A simple text formatting syntax (# headings, **bold**, - lists) that converts to HTML; used in README files, docs and chat apps.
A powerful open-source relational database; with the pgvector extension it can also store and search embeddings.
Packaging an app with everything it needs so it runs the same way on any machine.
Red Hat's enterprise Kubernetes platform for building, deploying and running containerized apps (including AI workloads through OpenShift AI) on-premises or in any cloud.
A DNS record that makes one domain name an alias of another, for example pointing you.can-du-ai.com to husamalqawasmeh.github.io.
Cloudflare's serverless SQL database, built on SQLite, used with Cloudflare Workers.
Vercel's AI tool that generates web user interfaces and full-stack apps (React, Next.js) from a text prompt or image.
Practices and tools for deploying, monitoring and maintaining ML models in production.
When real-world input data changes over time from the training data, so model quality drops.

questions.q: What topics should an LLM engineer know?
questions.followup: Pick one and explain how you measured or sized it in a real project.
questions.answer: Benchmarking and evals, latency (time to first token, time per output token) and throughput (tokens per second, concurrency), capabilities (text, vision, voice, video, tool calling, structured output, context window), hardware sizing (VRAM for weights plus KV cache, RAM, GPU type), optimization (quantization, batching, caching, speculative decoding), serving (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, Ollama), context engineering and RAG, fine-tuning (LoRA), cost, safety and production monitoring. For the follow-up, give one real measurement, for example "p95 TTFT dropped from 2.1 s to 0.6 s after enabling prefix caching".

questions.q: How would you size the GPUs and VRAM to serve a 70B model to 100 concurrent users with 8K-token contexts?
questions.followup: Which levers (quantization, KV cache, batching, a smaller model) would you pull first to cut cost, and what would you measure?
questions.answer: Weights: 70B in FP16 is about 140 GB, in FP8 about 70 GB, in 4-bit about 35-40 GB. KV cache: for a Llama-70B-style model (80 layers, 8 KV heads with GQA, head size 128, FP16) about 0.33 MB per token, so 100 users × 8K tokens ≈ 800K tokens ≈ 260 GB at full use. Total in FP16 ≈ 400+ GB, for example a node of 8 × 80 GB GPUs with tensor parallelism; FP8 weights and FP8 KV cache can roughly halve it. Levers in order: FP8/4-bit quantization (check evals), FP8 KV cache and PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching, then a smaller or distilled model. Measure quality, p95 latency, throughput and cost per million tokens.

questions.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput for an LLM service, and how do you trade one against the other?
questions.followup: Which metrics (TTFT, time per output token, p95) would you put on the dashboard, and why?
questions.answer: Latency is how long one user waits: time to first token plus time per output token × output length. Throughput is how much work the whole system does: tokens or requests per second across all users. Bigger batches raise throughput and lower cost per token but can raise each user's latency, so set a latency target (for example p95 TTFT under 1 s) and maximize throughput within it. Dashboard: TTFT and time per output token at p50/p95/p99, tokens per second, requests per second, queue time, GPU utilization, error rate and cost per million tokens.

questions.q: What topics should an AI engineer know, and which are your strongest and weakest?
questions.followup: What are you doing to close the gap in your weakest area?
questions.answer: Programming (Python, Git, APIs, SQL, testing), math basics (linear algebra, probability, statistics), ML fundamentals (data splits, overfitting, metrics), deep learning and Transformers, LLMs (prompting, RAG, agents, MCP, fine-tuning), data engineering, evaluation, MLOps/LLMOps (CI/CD, Docker, Kubernetes, monitoring), cloud and GPUs, responsible and secure AI, and product sense. Name a real strength with an example, and an honest weakness with a concrete plan (a course, a side project, a certification, a date).

questions.q: What is the difference between an AI engineer, an ML engineer, a data scientist and an LLM engineer?
questions.followup: Which of these roles fits the work you want to do, and why?
questions.answer: Data scientist: analyzes data and runs experiments to answer business questions. ML engineer: trains, deploys and scales ML models (pipelines, serving, MLOps). AI engineer: builds products on top of AI models, often foundation models through APIs or open weights, with strong software engineering, integration and evals. LLM engineer: an AI engineer focused on LLMs (prompting, RAG, agents, serving, GPU sizing). The roles overlap and titles differ by company; pick the one that matches the work you enjoy and give a reason.

questions.q: Walk me through taking an AI feature from idea to production.
questions.followup: How do you know it is working after launch, and what would make you roll it back?
questions.answer: 1) Define the problem, users and a success metric. 2) Check data and feasibility; build a quick prototype. 3) Build an eval set and a baseline. 4) Iterate on prompts, RAG or model choice until evals pass. 5) Add guardrails, security, privacy review and cost limits. 6) Ship behind a feature flag to a small group or A/B test. 7) Monitor quality, latency, cost, errors and feedback with tracing. Roll back if quality or business metrics drop, costs spike, or safety or privacy incidents happen.

questions.q: What is a container, and why do AI and LLM applications need containerization?
questions.followup: How would you give a container GPU access, and where would you keep the model weights?
questions.answer: A container packages an app with its code, runtime and libraries so it runs the same everywhere; it shares the host OS kernel, so it is lighter than a VM. AI needs it because Python, PyTorch, CUDA and driver versions must match exactly; containers give reproducibility, portability across clouds, ready-made serving images (vLLM, TGI, Triton, NVIDIA NIM), scaling with Kubernetes and sandboxing for agent-generated code. GPU access: install NVIDIA drivers and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host and run with --gpus all (or the GPU operator on Kubernetes). Keep model weights outside the image on a mounted volume or download them at start.

questions.q: What is quantization, and what are the trade-offs of running a model in 8-bit or 4-bit?
questions.followup: How would you check that a quantized model is still good enough for production?
questions.answer: Quantization stores weights (and sometimes activations or KV cache) with fewer bits: FP16 → 8-bit → 4-bit. 8-bit halves memory with almost no quality loss; 4-bit cuts memory by about 4× and speeds up decoding, but may lose some quality, especially on math, code and long contexts; below 4 bits loss grows. Methods: GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes, FP8, GGUF for llama.cpp. To check it: run the same eval set on original and quantized models, compare scores, spot-check outputs, test long-context and edge cases, and measure latency and memory before production.

questions.q: What is NVIDIA DGX Spark, and how does it compare with a Mac Studio, an AMD Strix Halo mini PC or a PC with an RTX 5090 for local LLM work?
questions.followup: For a 70B model, which would you buy and why: memory size, memory bandwidth or software support?
questions.answer: DGX Spark is NVIDIA's desktop AI computer with the GB10 Grace Blackwell chip and 128 GB unified memory (about 273 GB/s), running the full CUDA stack; it fits models up to about 200B parameters in FP4 and is great for prototyping and fine-tuning. Mac Studio M3 Ultra: up to 512 GB and about 819 GB/s, so faster generation on big models, but no CUDA. AMD Strix Halo mini PCs: up to 128 GB at about 256 GB/s, cheaper, ROCm. RTX 5090: only 32 GB but about 1.8 TB/s, fastest when the model fits. For a 70B model: memory size decides if it fits (4-bit ≈ 40 GB), bandwidth decides speed, software decides ease; for CUDA work pick Spark, for fastest local chat at 70B a Mac Studio, for small models an RTX 5090.

questions.q: Why do AI video generators struggle with physics, and what kinds of errors do they make?
questions.followup: How would you measure physical correctness, and what would you change in data or training to improve it?
questions.answer: Video models learn how pixels usually look and move, not physical laws; they have no built-in 3D world, mass or forces, and rare events are thin in training data. Errors: objects vanishing or merging, wrong gravity, bodies passing through each other, missing cause and effect (a bite with no mark), liquids appearing or disappearing, morphing hands, and drift over long clips. Measure with physics benchmarks (Physics-IQ, VideoPhy, PhyGenBench) and human review. Improve with better-labeled data, synthetic data from physics simulators and game engines, 3D-aware world models, rewards for physical correctness and longer context for consistency.

questions.q: What is CoWoS, and why has advanced packaging become so important for AI hardware?
questions.followup: How does packaging capacity affect GPU supply and the cost of running large models?
questions.answer: CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) is TSMC's 2.5D packaging: the GPU die and HBM stacks sit side by side on a silicon (or organic) interposer with very dense wiring, mounted on a package substrate. AI accelerators are limited by memory bandwidth, and HBM only reaches terabytes per second when it sits right next to the GPU with thousands of short links. CoWoS also gets past the reticle limit by joining several dies, as in NVIDIA Blackwell B200 (two GPU dies on CoWoS-L). Since 2023 CoWoS and HBM capacity, not die production, have been the main bottleneck for AI GPU supply, so TSMC keeps doubling capacity. For engineers this means GPU availability and price depend on the whole supply chain, which affects cloud pricing and hardware planning.

questions.q: What is ASML's High-NA EUV machine, and why does it matter for AI chips?
questions.followup: What are its trade-offs (cost, exposure field size) and how do they affect very large AI accelerators?
questions.answer: ASML is the only maker of EUV lithography machines, which print the smallest features on leading-edge chips using 13.5 nm light from a tin plasma, steered by mirrors in a vacuum. Standard EUV has a numerical aperture of 0.33; High-NA EUV (EXE:5000/5200) raises it to 0.55, printing about 1.7x smaller features (about 8 nm resolution) and nearly 3x the density per exposure, and can replace costly multi-patterning. Smaller nodes give AI accelerators more compute per watt, lowering training and inference cost. Trade-offs: about $350-400 million per machine, and a half-size exposure field, so very large AI dies need stitching or multi-die designs with packaging like CoWoS. Intel adopted it first; TSMC and Samsung plan it for later nodes. Export controls keep EUV out of China, making it a strategic part of the AI race.

questions.q: Explain the AI chip supply chain: what do NVIDIA, AMD, TSMC and CUDA each contribute, and what does "fabless" mean?
questions.followup: If you had to run LLMs on AMD instead of NVIDIA GPUs, what would change in your software stack?
questions.answer: NVIDIA and AMD are fabless: they design GPUs but do not own fabs. TSMC is the leading foundry that manufactures their chips on advanced nodes (4N, N3, N2) and packages them with HBM using CoWoS; ASML supplies the EUV machines the fabs need. CUDA is NVIDIA's software platform (kernels plus libraries like cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL, TensorRT) that PyTorch and most AI tools use, and its ecosystem is NVIDIA's main moat. AMD competes with Instinct GPUs (MI300X, MI355X) that offer more HBM per GPU, and with ROCm/HIP as its CUDA alternative. Moving to AMD: use ROCm builds of PyTorch and inference engines like vLLM or SGLang, port custom CUDA kernels with HIP or rewrite them in Triton, replace NCCL with RCCL, and test performance and stability because library coverage is narrower.

questions.q: How would you evaluate an AI agent, and how do you make sure an LLM-as-a-judge can be trusted?
questions.followup: Your eval score went from 80% to 84% after a prompt change. Would you ship it? What would you check first?
questions.answer: Evaluate the outcome and the path. Outcome: task success measured by checking the final state (tests pass, record updated). Trajectory: right tools, correct arguments, number of steps, loops, recovery from errors. Also cost, latency and safety (forbidden actions, data leaks, prompt injection). Agents are non-deterministic, so run each task several times and report pass rates, including reliability across runs. Build a task suite from real user requests and add every production failure. For an LLM judge: give a clear rubric, prefer binary or pairwise verdicts, ask for reasoning before the verdict, one criterion per call, and swap answer order to cancel position bias. Calibrate it on a hand-labelled sample and measure agreement (accuracy, Cohen's kappa) before trusting it, and re-check when the judge model changes. For 80% to 84%: check the sample size and confidence interval, compare paired results case by case, look at what broke as well as what improved, and check cost and latency before shipping.

questions.q: A model predicts fraud probability. How do you choose the threshold and design the decision process around it?
questions.followup: How would you include an LLM in this process safely, for example to explain or review flagged cases?
questions.answer: First check the model is calibrated (predicted probabilities match real rates) using a reliability diagram, and fix it with Platt scaling or isotonic regression if needed. Then put money on the errors: cost of a false positive (blocked good customer, review time) versus a false negative (fraud loss). Flag a case when probability × fraud loss > (1 - probability) × false-positive cost, or sweep thresholds on validation data and pick the one with the lowest total expected cost. Look at precision and recall at that point, not accuracy, because fraud is rare. Use bands: auto-approve low scores, auto-block very high ones, and send the middle to human review within the team's capacity. Keep hard rules (limits, sanctions lists) in deterministic code or DMN tables. Monitor drift and re-tune over time, and A/B test threshold changes. An LLM can summarise the evidence and draft a reason for reviewers, using structured output, while the decision limits stay in code, humans approve high-impact cases, and everything is logged for audit.

questions.q: How would you build an AI strategy for a mid-sized company that has many AI experiments but little business value?
questions.followup: Which three use cases would you pick first, and how would you decide?
questions.answer: Start with the business: agree 2-3 outcomes with leadership (for example lower service cost, faster sales cycles, fewer errors) and name an executive owner. Take stock of current pilots, data, tools and risks. Score candidate use cases on value, feasibility, data readiness, risk, adoption effort and time to value; pick 2-5 with clear owners, baselines and a path to production, ideally in one lighthouse area, and stop pilots with no value story. Decide build, buy or partner per component: buy commodity tools, build where proprietary data or workflows give an edge, keep a model gateway to avoid lock-in. Set up a hub-and-spoke model: a central platform and governance team with AI people embedded in business units. Put governance in place early (AI policy, inventory, risk tiers, human review rules, NIST AI RMF or ISO 42001, EU AI Act where relevant). Redesign workflows, train staff, use champions. Track adoption, operational and financial KPIs against the baseline, report quarterly and scale what works.

questions.q: Many reports say most AI pilots fail to deliver returns. Why does this happen, and how would you avoid it?
questions.followup: How would you measure ROI for a customer-support AI assistant, including its full cost?
questions.answer: Common causes: starting from technology instead of a business problem; too many disconnected pilots; weak or inaccessible data; tools bolted onto old processes instead of redesigned workflows; no learning loop, so systems do not improve from feedback; unclear owners and no baseline; underestimated cost; and little change management, so people do not adopt the tool. MIT NANDA's 2025 GenAI Divide report and Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by 2027 both point to unclear value, integration and risk controls. To avoid it: tie each use case to a measurable outcome and owner, check data readiness first, integrate into the real workflow, design human-in-the-loop review, evaluate quality continuously, plan adoption and training, and stop projects that miss milestones. For a support assistant: baseline handle time, resolution rate, CSAT and cost per ticket; compare with a control group; count tokens, licences, integration, evaluation, monitoring and training in the cost; ROI = (value - cost) / cost.
